summary:
North Chungcheong province stands under the national framework of South Korea, where gender identity and gender expression are not criminalised in civilian life and consensual same-sex conduct between civilians is legal. The exception is the armed forces: Military Criminal Act article 92-6 criminalises consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel with up to two years' imprisonment, the Constitutional Court upheld the provision in 2023, and a gay soldier received a six-month sentence in 2017. Transgender people are excluded from military service altogether.

Legal gender recognition is available in South Korea and the surgery requirement is falling. On 8 May 2024 a court ruled against mandating sex-reassignment surgery as a condition of changing legal sex status, holding for five plaintiffs assigned male at birth who had been on hormone therapy for years that forcing surgery violates physical integrity and that outdated judicial guidelines cannot ground dismissals. The Supreme Court has also allowed a transgender person with minor children to change gender in the family relations register. Trans visitors hold a documented, judicially enforced right to public restrooms: on 2 July 2024 the Seoul Central District Court issued a final, unappealed ruling that police advice telling a transgender plaintiff undergoing gender correction to avoid public restrooms for a period infringed personal rights, awarding 300,000 won in symbolic compensation against the state.

There is no comprehensive South Korean anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity, so services, employment and accommodation carry no statutory protection on those grounds. In healthcare the National Human Rights Commission of Korea flagged a transgender blind spot in hospitalisation in November 2023, after the Ministry of Health and Welfare rejected a request to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients on the grounds that accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult. There is no same-sex marriage, which matters to a visitor travelling with a partner; the Constitutional Court's landmark 2024 ruling extended recognition of same-sex partners' healthcare rights in that specific area.

The province's only trans-specific documented event is the death of Byun Hee-soo, 23, South Korea's first transgender soldier, who was discharged for gender-affirming surgery after her landmark military challenge was rejected in July 2020. She was found dead at her home in Cheongju on 3 March 2021, a counsellor having raised the alarm on 28 February, and her death triggered national debate on the treatment of trans troops.

The handling of that death is the province's distinguishing finding. The initial classification of the death as natural stood for three years before a national review board recognised it as service-related in April 2024.

Aftermath evidence runs in the direction of national protection rather than regional law. Public grief and demands for LGBT protections surged after 3 March 2021, the National Human Rights Commission honoured her, and prosecutors and activists called for an anti-discrimination bill, its eighth introduction since 2007, with a June 2020 draft that included gender-identity provisions; society-wide discourse about responsibility followed.

For a visitor on the ground, no traveler-facing enforcement action, arrest, incident, or hostility directed at visitors is documented in these sources for North Chungcheong, and no repeat-violence data exists for this unit. A trans visitor's exposure therefore tracks the national baseline, with the institutional-handling finding informing rather than elevating the assessment. No severe incident involving a trans visitor is documented in these sources.

No visitor document requirements, border-screening practice, or marriage or partner-travel provision is recorded for this province.
tangentialFactors:
The province's −0.02 deviation below the national score rests on a single dated and located incident rather than a pattern of encounters between trans people and local authorities. One event of this kind carries the whole regional signal, so the deviation should be read as an institutional-handling indicator, not as a measure of street-level risk to visitors.

The incident generated documented national-protection pressure without producing any change to provincial law: calls for an anti-discrimination bill, an honour from the National Human Rights Commission, and a society-wide responsibility discourse. South Korea still has no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity, so the pressure recorded here has not translated into statutory protection for services, employment or accommodation.

Organised conservative opposition to LGBT rights is active nationally, and Human Rights Watch's 2025 world report records persistent documented discrimination against LGBT people while also noting a relatively positive overall record for free media and civil society. Both conditions shape the environment a visitor enters.

For comparison, Seoul's established LGBTQ+ neighbourhoods are broadly positive, which is relevant to a visitor deciding where to base excursions into the province. The surrounding context still requires care because of the absence of a national anti-discrimination law and the presence of active organised opposition.

The April 2024 recognition of her death as service-related, after three years classified as natural, is a resident-facing matter of veterans' status, benefits and official record, and it followed sustained pressure from the National Human Rights Commission of Korea, prosecutors and activists.

Residents share the national position on legal gender recognition: the 8 May 2024 ruling removed sex-reassignment surgery as a condition of changing legal sex status for plaintiffs assigned male at birth on long-term hormone therapy, the Supreme Court permits gender change in the family relations register even where minor children are involved, and the 2 July 2024 Seoul Central District Court judgment protects use of public restrooms against police advice to the contrary.

Residents have no statutory protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity in employment, services or accommodation, and hospitalisation guidance for transgender patients has not been drafted after the Ministry of Health and Welfare declined to do so in 2023. Same-sex marriage is not available; the Constitutional Court's 2024 ruling covers same-sex partners' healthcare rights only.
